###### Abstract

AI-based question-answering systems are increasingly used for user
support, including at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities.
However, existing systems lack a systematic, deployment-oriented
approach for evaluating final-answer quality and attributing failures to
specific components. They also remain largely static after deployment,
apart from periodic knowledge-base updates.

We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline for
HPC user support. AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a
fine-grained level, identifies whether failures arise from missing
knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and
routes each failure to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core
combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test
that distinguishes information missing from the documentation corpus
from information present but not retrieved. We further introduce a
controlled harness-training process that uses expert references, null
edits, and explicit ship, revert, or decline decisions to improve the
diagnostic pipeline reliably.

Across 2,174 support turns, AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from
41.4% to 14.2%, while harness training improved expert agreement from
108/150 to 123/150 turns. These results demonstrate a governed form of
self-evolution in which production evidence drives targeted system
improvements. By turning production interactions into fine-grained
diagnoses and actionable repairs, AskALCF provides a systematic
foundation for continuously improving deployed AI support systems beyond
knowledge-base updates alone.

###### Index Terms: 

high performance computing, artificial intelligence, natural language
processing, information retrieval, knowledge management

## I Introduction

Leadership computing facilities support thousands of users across
systems whose hardware, software and operating procedures change
continuously. New partitions come online, programming environments
evolve, and compiler, driver and library versions change between
maintenance cycles. At the same time, the information users need is
distributed across facility guides, vendor manuals, software
documentation, release notes and separate web portals. Finding the right
information is therefore difficult even when it has been documented.
Together, rapid change, fragmented documentation and growing demand
create a persistent support burden for both users and facility staff.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a promising way to make
this support more accessible. Systems such as AskHPC \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]
and chatHPC \[[2](#bib.bib2)\], HyCE’s HPC-oriented RAG
architecture \[[3](#bib.bib37)\], and recent cross-facility
studies \[[4](#bib.bib36)\] show that language models can answer
technical questions using facility documentation. These systems
represent an important advance over static documentation search: users
can ask questions in natural language and receive an immediate,
context-aware response.

However, current systems remain limited in two important ways. First,
detecting a poor answer does not reveal how to fix it. The same visible
error may result from missing documentation, failed retrieval, an
inadequate prompt, model behavior, or a broken tool call. These causes
belong to different teams and require different repairs. A single
quality score can identify that an answer is weak, but it cannot
identify who should act or what they should change.

Second, deployed assistants make little systematic use of the evidence
they accumulate. Every interaction records a real user need, the
material retrieved for it, and the answer produced. Support tickets
provide another source of operational knowledge: they capture problems
that may require an existing answer, reproduction on ALCF systems, or
intervention by a system owner. Yet chatbot logs and support tickets are
typically handled as separate records rather than as evidence for
continuously improving the support system.

We present AskALCF, an agentic support and improvement framework that
connects these two channels. Interactive questions are answered by a
deployed RAG service, while a diagnostic pipeline analyzes the resulting
logs and routes failures to the component that can address them. Support
tickets are classified by the type of resolution they require, and
responses are drafted for expert review. A shared knowledge-management
process collects lessons from both channels and turns them into reviewed
updates to the documentation corpus. Together, these four components
allow the system to learn from production use, improve its diagnostic
rules and prompts, and accumulate reusable knowledge. We refer to this
controlled process as _governed self-evolution_: the system proposes and
evaluates improvements, while human experts retain authority over
responses and deployed changes.

The central idea is to distinguish an answer’s visible symptom from its
underlying cause. In particular, AskALCF asks two separate questions:
whether the retrieved passages were sufficient to answer the user, and
whether the required information existed anywhere in the documentation
corpus. This distinction, inspired by sufficient-context
evaluation \[[5](#bib.bib14)\], separates missing knowledge from failed
retrieval. Combined with evidence about the answer, model and tool
execution, it allows the system to route a failure to one of five
component owners rather than returning only a quality score. An agent
judge independently audits the route, while ALCF experts provide the
final reference for disputed or uncertain cases.

This changes the role of an AI support assistant. Instead of treating
each interaction as an isolated question-answer exchange, AskALCF treats
production use as evidence for improving the support process itself. The
result is a governed loop from user request, to diagnosis, to repair, to
reviewed knowledge. The significance is not simply that the assistant
can produce another answer; it is that the system can identify an
actionable repair, direct it to the right owner, and preserve the
resulting lesson for future users.

We evaluate this approach on 2,174 production support turns. The
diagnostic pipeline reduces failures that cannot be assigned to an owner
from 41.4% to 14.2%. A human-guided improvement process increases
agreement with a frozen three-expert reference from 108/150 to 123/150
turns. Controlled repair experiments further show that the resulting
diagnoses can guide effective prompt and documentation changes.
Together, these results demonstrate that production support evidence can
be converted into measurable and actionable system improvements.

  prompting, model behavior and tool execution, and routes each failure
  to the component owner who can address it.
- •

  (§[III-B4](#S3.SS2.SSS4 "III-B4 Agentic Audit ‣ III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support"),

Scope. The improvement loop is implemented and evaluated through expert
review. We diagnose production interactions, author targeted repairs,
and measure their effects in controlled experiments. No
CODEOWNERS-approved knowledge change has yet been merged into the
deployed corpus and re-indexed. We therefore report measured offline
improvements, not a claim that the production system has already
modified itself autonomously.

## II Background and Related Work

### II-A HPC Assistants and RAG Diagnosis

AskHPC and chatHPC \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2)\] answer user
questions from facility documentation, with chatHPC also supporting
script generation. HyCE \[[3](#bib.bib37)\] extends retrieval to
HPC-specific operational data, while cross-facility studies show that
support behavior does not transfer cleanly between
sites \[[4](#bib.bib36)\]. These systems demonstrate the value of
language models for HPC support, but their principal output is an answer
rather than a diagnosis or repair path.

Existing RAG evaluations measure complementary aspects of retrieval and
generation. RAGAS \[[6](#bib.bib10)\] and RAGChecker \[[7](#bib.bib12)\]
provide multi-dimensional evaluation, while citation-based methods
assess whether claims are supported by retrieved
evidence \[[8](#bib.bib11)\]. The Sufficient Context test asks whether
the passages returned for a question contain enough information to
answer it \[[5](#bib.bib14)\]. AskALCF extends this idea to two scopes:
the passages returned in production and the complete corpus. The
difference distinguishes a retrieval failure from a documentation gap
and therefore identifies the component owner who can act.

Other work uses relevance or sufficiency judgments to adapt retrieval
during a turn \[[9](#bib.bib16), [10](#bib.bib15)\], and taxonomies
describe recurring RAG engineering failures \[[11](#bib.bib22)\]. These
methods improve an answer or characterize a failure, but do not connect
production evidence to a facility support workflow. Our contribution is
an operational diagnosis: the two-scope sufficiency test is combined
with answer and tool evidence to assign each production turn to a
component-level route and a corresponding repair owner.

### II-B Agentic Evaluation and Governance

Agent-as-a-Judge systems use tools to acquire evidence before producing
a verdict \[[12](#bib.bib28), [13](#bib.bib29)\]. This capability is
useful for failure attribution because an agent can inspect evidence
that was absent from the original interaction. However, LLM judges
remain sensitive to position, self-preference, and other systematic
biases \[[14](#bib.bib20), [15](#bib.bib26)\]; self-reported confidence
is also an unreliable indicator of correctness \[[16](#bib.bib23)\].
Executable software agents introduce a related governance problem: their
localize–repair–validate workflows require bounded tools and explicit
safety controls \[[17](#bib.bib19), [18](#bib.bib21)\].

Agentic failure-attribution systems similarly use tools to localize
faults in execution traces \[[19](#bib.bib30), [20](#bib.bib31)\].
Existing governance strategies commonly rely on confidence thresholds,
escalation, or multiple judges \[[21](#bib.bib24), [22](#bib.bib25)\].
These strategies are difficult to apply when confidence is not
calibrated to correctness.

AskALCF therefore combines deterministic and agentic evaluation. An
ordered rule tree assigns the initial failure route, an agent judge
independently probes the corpus, and a rule-conditioned gate limits when
the judge may change the route. Human review remains mandatory for
ticket responses, knowledge changes, and generated repairs. Our
contribution is the division of authority: the judge may overturn only
decisions based on evidence it can independently test, while experts
retain control over every production-facing action.

### II-C Human-Guided Self-Improvement

Self-improving agents commonly update an internal memory or skill
library from their own traces \[[23](#bib.bib17), [24](#bib.bib18)\],
while systems such as DSPy and GEPA optimize prompts or language-model
programs against an evaluation objective \[[25](#bib.bib8),
[26](#bib.bib32)\]. Recent systems also learn skills from operational
support traces or maintain documentation through agentic
feedback \[[27](#bib.bib38), [28](#bib.bib39)\]. These approaches differ
primarily in what they modify and who determines whether a change is
acceptable.

Pipeline optimizers can also propagate natural-language feedback through
prompts and agent trajectories \[[29](#bib.bib9), [30](#bib.bib33)\].
However, small prompt changes can interact with nondeterministic
generation and produce apparent gains that do not
replicate \[[31](#bib.bib35), [32](#bib.bib34)\]. A self-improvement
claim therefore requires both a stable reference and controls for
run-to-run variation.

In AskALCF, domain experts provide both corrected routes and written
rationales. These observations motivate bounded changes to diagnostic
rules, judge instructions, and ALCF knowledge. Each change is evaluated
against a frozen, session-disjoint expert reference before acceptance.
The resulting process improves the surrounding harness rather than model
weights, while human reviewers retain authority over every
production-facing change. Our contribution is a governed self-evolution
protocol that turns expert explanations into testable harness changes,
records accepted and rejected arms, and promotes a change only when its
target cases improve and its controls remain stable.

## III System Design and Implementation

At the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF), users reach AskALCF
through two channels. Short how-to questions arrive through web chat or
MCP \[[33](#bib.bib3)\] and need an immediate answer. The service covers
Polaris and Aurora and sends model requests through the ALCF Argo
inference gateway. Problem reports arrive by email and become support
tickets. A ticket may be answered from existing knowledge, sent to an
agent to reproduce and repair the problem on real HPC resources, or
routed to the team responsible for a system-level fix.

These needs motivate four pillars. Pillar 1 answers chatbot questions,
and Pillar 3 analyzes the resulting logs to identify failures and
improve the service. Pillar 4 triages support tickets and directs each
one to an appropriate resolution path. Pillar 2 collects lessons from
both channels and turns them into reviewed knowledge updates. Together,
the four pillars connect immediate assistance, failure analysis, ticket
resolution, and knowledge curation in a single human-governed
improvement loop. Because a ticket’s _complete_ flag does not reliably
indicate resolution
(§[V-B](#S5.SS2 "V-B RQ1: Does Log Analysis Produce Actionable Diagnoses? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")),
Pillar 4 re-triages every ticket from its content.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 1: AskALCF connects two support channels to a governed improvement
loop. A user query enters Pillar 1 (1), whose trace is analyzed by
Pillar 3 (2). Confirmed knowledge gaps go to Pillar 2 (3), while other
failures go to their component owners (3b). A ticket enters Pillar 4
(0), which drafts a reply for staff review (4) and sends reusable fixes
to Pillar 2 (5). Pillar 2 opens a pull request (6); after human
approval, the merge trigger re-indexes the corpus (7). That final
trigger has not yet fired.

### III-A The Four Subsystems

Pillar 1 — Q&A service. This deployed RAG service indexes a curated
corpus of facility user guides, vendor documentation and other
operational materials in Milvus \[[34](#bib.bib7)\]. For each question,
it retrieves relevant passages and sends them to a language model as
context for answer generation. It logs the question, answer, retrieved
passages, tool calls and retrieval score. Pillar 3 uses this record to
evaluate what the production system actually saw.

Pillar 3 — Log analysis. Pillar 3 examines each failing Pillar 1 turn
and assigns one of five causes: knowledge, retrieval, prompt, model or
tools_mcp. A knowledge failure means that the required information is
absent from the indexed corpus, whereas a retrieval failure means that
the information exists but was not returned to the model. A prompt
failure occurs when the system instructions induce inappropriate
behavior, such as unnecessary clarification. A model failure occurs when
sufficient context and appropriate instructions are available but the
model produces an incorrect or unsupported answer. A tools_mcp failure
arises when an external tool, MCP service or its invocation fails. We
use no_failure when the evidence supports a healthy response and unknown
when the available evidence cannot support an attribution. Knowledge
failures go to Pillar 2; the others go to the teams that own the
affected components. The deterministic rule tree makes the initial
decision
(§[III-B](#S3.SS2 "III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")).
LLMs provide evidence at fixed points in the tree, and an agent judge
audits the final route instead of replacing the tree
(§[III-B4](#S3.SS2.SSS4 "III-B4 Agentic Audit ‣ III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")).

Pillar 4 — Ticket resolution. Pillar 4 assigns each ticket to one of
three resolution paths: answer it from existing knowledge, reproduce and
repair the reported problem by running a real job at the ALCF, or route
a system-level problem to the team that owns the affected service. It
then drafts a response explaining the answer, tested repair or handoff.
Support staff at the ALCF must review and approve the draft before it is
sent to the user.

Ticket ingestion, classification and response drafting are implemented.
For a reproducible problem, ingestion also produces a validated record
containing the failing job, error signature and rerun script. The agent
that consumes this record and runs the job on a live allocation has not
yet been exercised. That path uses Apptainer \[[35](#bib.bib6)\],
Spack \[[36](#bib.bib5)\], CodeAct-style \[[17](#bib.bib19)\] functions
and Parsl \[[37](#bib.bib4)\], and is limited to three build attempts,
thirty minutes of wall time and one node-hour.

Pillar 2 — Knowledge curation. Pillar 2 turns confirmed knowledge gaps
and reusable ticket lessons into updates to the corpus used by Pillar 1.
A writer drafts each change, and a reviewer either rejects it or
prepares it as a pull request. Drafting and dry-run application are
operational. Opening a pull request is marked $`\square`$ because the
service account cannot merge it. Every change therefore requires
CODEOWNERS approval before it can reach the deployed corpus. No
knowledge-writer pull request has yet passed that review, so the
merge-triggered Milvus re-indexing path has not fired.

### III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution

Pillar 3 converts each logged interaction into a diagnosis and an
actionable route.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
summarizes the workflow. Layer A evaluates the answer, while Layer B
evaluates retrieval without seeing the answer. An ordered rule tree
combines this evidence and assigns the turn to a component owner. An
agent judge audits that decision, and a human expert reviews disputed or
uncertain cases. The resulting expert labels are then used to improve
the rule tree and the judge skills.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 2: The diagnostic workflow and its expert-review loop. Layers B and
A produce retrieval and answer evidence, respectively. The ordered rule
tree (3) assigns the initial route, and the agent judge (4) audits that
decision. A human expert reviews the evidence and both rationales (5);

#### III-B1 Answer-Quality Evidence (Layer A)

Layer A computes four answer-quality signals and one deterministic scope
check. All entailment decisions use the same three-class judge
(entailment, neutral or contradiction), which keeps differences between
signals attributable to their evidence rather than to different judging
functions.

correctness measures the fraction of answer claims supported by evidence
retrieved separately for each claim. faithfulness applies the same test
to the context originally shown to the model. Their difference is
therefore diagnostic: an answer may contain correct information that was
not supported by its supplied context.

grounding checks whether paths, modules and documentation URLs cited in
the answer exist. Following the fabricated-citation setting of
ALCE \[[8](#bib.bib11)\], it returns _found_, _mangled_real_ or
_fabricated_. The middle value indicates that the artifact exists but
was damaged during chunking, which is a retrieval defect rather than a
fabricated citation. An answer with no such citation receives n/a, not
zero. completeness follows the recall formulation of
RAGChecker \[[7](#bib.bib12)\]. Finally, facility_scope is a
deterministic lexicon check that rejects answers referring to another
facility or to an unsupported GPU stack.

The abstention detector distinguishes _full_, _partial_ and _no_
abstention. It removes fenced code, references and clarifying questions
before counting substantive claims. Only a full abstention exempts the
answer-quality signals. Ambiguous cases are treated as partial
abstentions, because incorrectly exempting a substantive answer could
hide a genuine failure.

#### III-B2 Retrieval and Corpus Sufficiency (Layer B)

Layer B separates two questions that are often combined. $`R`$ asks
whether the top-$`k`$ passages returned in production were sufficient.
$`C`$ asks whether the required information existed anywhere in the
corpus. $`R`$ follows the Sufficient Context test \[[5](#bib.bib14)\];
$`C`$ extends that test to a wider candidate set obtained from expanded
dense queries and BM25 search.

The two verdicts determine the responsible component. If $`R`$ is true,
retrieval was sufficient and the rule tree evaluates the generation-side
evidence. If $`R`$ is false but $`C`$ is true, the corpus contains the
answer and the failure is assigned to retrieval. If both are false, the
corpus lacks sufficient documentation and the failure is assigned to
knowledge. This distinction turns a sufficiency judgment into an
actionable work item.

Two constraints preserve that interpretation. First, Layer B never sees
the generated answer; otherwise it could not distinguish insufficient
retrieval from poor answer generation. Second, $`R`$ and $`C`$ use
different query policies. $`R`$ evaluates the query and passages used in
production. $`C`$ may use rewritten, goal-directed queries because it
tests corpus coverage rather than production retrieval. A relaxed
condition is therefore applied to $`R`$ only when supported by direct
production evidence.

For complex questions, $`C`$ is evaluated over answer requirements
rather than by asking whether a large collection of passages is
sufficient as a whole. The system decomposes the question into
requirements, marks the essential ones as _core_, and checks each core
requirement against the corpus. Core status is assigned without access
to coverage results, preventing a missing fact from being reclassified
as unimportant. If requirement extraction is malformed, all requirements
are treated as core, so the system fails conservatively.

We use semantic core requirements rather than a fixed fractional
coverage threshold, which would treat requirements of unequal importance
as interchangeable. The materiality judgment preserves the meaning of
corpus sufficiency across questions with different structures.

#### III-B3 Cause Attribution with an Ordered Rule Tree

The router is an ordered list of 28 rules with first-match semantics. A
predicate over a missing signal evaluates to false, so absent evidence
cannot trigger a route. The ordering in
Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
reflects four priorities. Service and tool failures are checked first,
because a backend outage should not be evaluated as a model-generated
answer. Deterministic facility-scope and clarification checks come next.
The $`R\times C`$ sufficiency pivot then separates retrieval and
knowledge failures. Answer-quality signals are considered only after
retrieval has been shown to be sufficient.

This ordering prevents answer-quality signals from absorbing retrieval
errors. When retrieval is insufficient, correctness and completeness are
also likely to be low. Evaluating those signals before the sufficiency
pivot would therefore assign retrieval failures to generation-side
components. Sufficient retrieval is treated as a prerequisite for
attributing a failure to answer generation.

On the generation side, the tree distinguishes how the answer used its
context from what the answer asserted. A fabricated citation or a
contradiction of the provided context is assigned to model, because the
required evidence was available but not used correctly. An answer that
remains faithful to its context but reaches an incorrect conclusion is
also assigned to model, for a different underlying reason. No
answer-quality score directly produces a prompt route, because a low
score alone cannot distinguish an inadequate instruction from inadequate
execution. Prompt routes arise from explicit policy checks performed
earlier in the tree.

The terminal outcomes no_failure and unknown have different meanings.
no_failure requires positive evidence that retrieval was sufficient and
the answer was faithful and correct. unknown indicates that no supported
attribution could be made. Keeping these outcomes separate distinguishes
a verified healthy turn from one that could not be evaluated. If a
deterministic signal conflicts with an unreliable judged signal, the
tree escalates the turn for human review rather than guessing.

Table [I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-B3 Cause Attribution with an Ordered Rule Tree ‣ III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
states the seven outcomes the tree can emit. Five are failure modes,
each naming the component that must change; two are terminal and
dispatch nobody. Every turn receives exactly one, so no turn leaves the
pipeline without a recorded disposition.

T and F are their truth values. Every scored turn receives exactly one
outcome.

Each top-level route retains more specific internal conditions for
engineering remediation. The paper reports the five component-level
causes for clarity. A cause is included only when a corresponding
detector can provide supporting evidence.

#### III-B4 Agentic Audit

After the rule tree assigns a route, an _agent judge_ audits the
decision. The judge does not replace the router. It checks whether the
evidence used by the matched rule supports the assigned cause. When it
disagrees, it identifies the disputed signal, producing a concrete item
for review rather than only a second route label.

We selected this audit design instead of a second generative router
because a second router would consume the same potentially unreliable
signals and would not provide an independent check on them.

The agent judge differs from the single-shot judges used to compute
individual signals. It runs a bounded probe loop over the corpus: it
lists candidate URLs, searches for evidence and reads selected chunks.
It can therefore find evidence that was absent from the production
retrieval result. As evaluated in
§[V-D](#S5.SS4 "V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support"),
this access is most useful when the rule tree reached a decision from
missing evidence.

Every judge call is logged, observations are size-limited, and probe
results are content-addressed and pinned for replay
(§[III-B5](#S3.SS2.SSS5 "III-B5 Reproducibility Controls ‣ III-B Log Analysis and Failure Attribution ‣ III System Design and Implementation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")).
These controls make each conclusion traceable to evidence the agent
actually inspected.

Authority is configured separately from judgment. The agent judge may
overturn the tree only for seven rule classes whose inputs it can
independently verify. For all other classes, its disagreement is
recorded for human review without changing the route. The gate depends
on the rule that fired, not on the judge’s self-reported confidence.
Section [V-D](#S5.SS4 "V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
evaluates this policy.

#### III-B5 Reproducibility Controls

The corpus probe used to compute $`C`$ expands each question into
sub-queries with an LLM call requesting temperature=0. The inference
gateway did not honor that setting: two otherwise identical runs
produced different expansion sets for all 78 tested questions, and the
resulting retrieval differences changed the final route for 16% of
turns.

We therefore cache each expansion under a hash of the query, model and
prompt. The cache is committed with the evaluation artifacts, making
expansions identical across runs and machines and reviewable as a diff.
Every result in this paper uses these pinned expansions.

## IV Human-Guided Self-Evolution

Production evidence does not change the system automatically. Instead,
experts review diagnoses, record corrections and propose bounded changes
to the rules, prompts or knowledge base. Each proposal is evaluated
against a fixed reference before it is accepted.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV-C Harness Training ‣ IV Human-Guided Self-Evolution ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
summarizes this cycle. We call the process _governed self-evolution_
because the system learns from its operation while people retain
authority over every consequential change.

### IV-A Expert Review and Reference Labels

A diagnostic route is a proposal rather than an action. The review
service therefore presents the evidence behind each route before a human
decision is recorded. It provides two role-scoped workspaces behind ALCF
single sign-on: an administrative workspace for reviewing chatbot
diagnoses and a staff workspace for reviewing ticket responses. Both
read immutable analysis artifacts and write decisions to a separate
append-only store.

For each chatbot turn, the administrative workspace shows the
answer-quality signals, the retrieval and corpus-sufficiency verdicts,
the matched rule, and the agent judge’s independent assessment.
Reviewers can accept the route, provide a corrected route and
explanation, or mark the sample as unsuitable for evaluation. An
unanswered item remains _uncertain_; it is never interpreted as
agreement. These decisions form the expert reference used for harness
training.

### IV-B Ticket Feedback and Knowledge Accumulation

The staff workspace applies the same approval principle to support
tickets. It re-triages each ticket, retrieves supporting documentation
and drafts a response with citations derived from the retrieved sources.
A support expert reviews the draft before exporting it to the expert’s
mail client; the system does not send messages automatically. Reusable
lessons and confirmed documentation gaps are then passed to the Pillar 2
writer–reviewer workflow. Any resulting corpus change requires
CODEOWNERS approval before merge and re-indexing.

### IV-C Harness Training

Harness training improves the diagnostic pipeline without changing model
weights. The editable harness consists of the rule tree, the judge
skills and the override gate. A human reviewer identifies a recurring
error, proposes one bounded change and names the turns that should
improve and the control turns that should remain unchanged. One complete
proposal-and-evaluation cycle is an _arm_.

As
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV-C Harness Training ‣ IV Human-Guided Self-Evolution ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
shows, each arm follows four steps: diagnose an error, pre-register its
target and control sets, run the revised harness, and either accept or
reject the change. Evaluation turns remain hidden from design decisions.
This process borrows the train/evaluation split and experiment ledger of
model training, but the trainable object is the surrounding software and
prompts rather than a model’s parameters.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 3: Human-guided harness training. Each proposed change is evaluated
as one arm with pre-registered target and control sets. A change is
accepted only when the target cases improve and the controls remain
stable. Evaluation cases are not used to propose, tune or select an arm.

#### IV-C1 Expert Reference and Data Split

We sampled 150 production sessions that did not overlap the development
pilot of
§[V-A](#S5.SS1 "V-A Evaluation Data and Development Pilot ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support").
Three domain scientists labelled the turns through the review interface,
and a fourth resolved disagreements. The router scores 171 turns across
these sessions; after excluding unsuitable records, 150 of them carry an
expert label and form the graded reference, split by session into 98
training and 52 evaluation turns. Session-level splitting prevents turns
from the same conversation from appearing on both sides.

The reference is generated from the reviewer records, content-hashed and
checked for drift before every evaluation. Reviewers provide both a
route and a written explanation. The explanation is essential: a
corrected label identifies the error, while the accompanying rationale
suggests what rule, instruction or evidence source should change.
Section [V](#S5 "V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
reports the resulting campaign and its accepted and rejected arms.

## V Evaluation

We evaluate four questions: whether log analysis produces actionable
diagnoses, whether human-guided harness training improves those
diagnoses, what the agent judge contributes, and whether the resulting
diagnoses lead to effective repairs. A 97-turn pilot supported taxonomy
development but not claims of generalization. Formal results use a
separate 150-turn multi-expert reference with a session-disjoint
training/evaluation split, together with the full corpus of 2,174 scored
turns.

### V-A Evaluation Data and Development Pilot

The router was first developed against 100 sessions collected between
February and July 2026, with one scored turn per session and
stratification across the five failure modes and no_failure. A single
author reviewed four questions per turn. Three turns were excluded as
unscoreable, leaving 97. Initial agreement was 53 of 97 (55%), including
ten false knowledge routes. Repairing the input signals increased
agreement to 77 of 97 (79%) and reduced false knowledge routes to four.

This result is developmental rather than confirmatory. The reviewer was
a single author, and the same turns informed the taxonomy, rule
ordering, and thresholds. We therefore use the separate 150-turn,
multi-expert reference described in
§[IV-C](#S4.SS3 "IV-C Harness Training ‣ IV Human-Guided Self-Evolution ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
for formal evaluation.

### V-B RQ1: Does Log Analysis Produce Actionable Diagnoses?

We applied the shipped router to the complete interaction corpus of
1,229 sessions and 2,174 scored assistant turns. Because the same turns
had been scored before harness training,
Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ V-B RQ1: Does Log Analysis Produce Actionable Diagnoses? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
provides a controlled comparison on identical inputs.

The principal improvement is a reduction in unattributed turns. The tree
could not assign a failure mode to 900 turns (41.4%) before training and
309 turns (14.2%) afterward; attributed turns therefore increased from
924 to 1,295. Run artifacts identify the mechanism: 729 turns in the
earlier run had no retrieval verdict, and 684 of them consequently fell
through to unknown. With the revised retrieval test, their largest
destinations are no_failure (198), knowledge (150), retrieval (147) and
prompt (75), while 106 remain unattributed. Thus, the change reflects
improved evidence coverage rather than a more permissive attribution
policy.

Raw turn counts can overstate recurring problems. The 1,229 sessions
contain 927 distinct opening questions, and the most frequent question
appears 33 times.
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-B RQ1: Does Log Analysis Produce Actionable Diagnoses? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
therefore also reports a deduplicated view. In total, 645 question
groups contain at least one non-healthy route; the five largest groups
account for 106 sessions and concern job and node counts, outbound
network access, login procedures, and job submission. This grouping
turns per-turn diagnoses into a support work queue without allowing
repeated questions to dominate it.

Two caveats travel with every cell. The smallest cells are not findings:
tools_mcp, at 4.7% raw and 3.6% deduplicated, is too thin a slice to
read as a rate. And the accuracy of
§[V-C](#S5.SS3 "V-C RQ2: Does Human-Guided Training Improve the Diagnostic? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
is established on 150 expert-labelled turns and nowhere else. The other
2,024 turns carry no reference, and the labelled slate was stratified,
not uniformly drawn, so that accuracy cannot be carried onto this table.

Ticket analysis provides a complementary view of support demand. Across
2,211 ticket threads, 18% of those flagged complete were not actually
resolved, while 319 resolved threads were never flagged. The ticket
system’s status field is therefore an unreliable proxy for outcome,
supporting the need to re-triage tickets from their content before
routing follow-up work.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 4: The same 2,174 turns scored before and after harness training,
on identical input. Turns the router could not attribute fall from 900

### V-C RQ2: Does Human-Guided Training Improve the Diagnostic?

Sixteen harness arms were evaluated against the frozen expert reference:
three were accepted, nine were rejected, and four were reference arms
(the baseline, a null control and two replication draws).
Table [II](#S5.T2 "TABLE II ‣ V-C RQ2: Does Human-Guided Training Improve the Diagnostic? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
reports the accepted path. Agreement rises from 108/150 to 123/150
turns. On the session-disjoint evaluation split, it rises from 35/52
(67%) to 40/52 (77%).

| Arm | Change                          | training (98) | eval. (52) | all |
| --- | ------------------------------- | ------------- | ---------- | --- |
| —   | baseline, gate closed           | 73            | 35         | 108 |
| A1  | rule-conditioned judge gate     | 80            | 37         | 117 |
| A2  | sufficiency $`+`$ clarification | 81            | 39         | 120 |
| A3  | stricter clarification rules    | 83            | 40         | 123 |

TABLE II: The accepted harness changes, scored against the frozen expert
reference. Evaluation turns were not used to propose or select an arm.

The first arm changed judge authority according to the rule that fired.
It corrected nine expert-labelled routes without introducing a
regression. The next two arms refined the sufficiency and clarification
signals consumed by the tree. The rejected arms generally attempted to
change a judge’s conclusion without changing the evidence available to
it. The accepted arms instead changed how existing evidence was
interpreted or combined.

Small aggregate changes require a null control. A semantically neutral
edit still changed 9 and 11 of the 171 scored routes in two replicates
because changing prompt bytes bypassed cached responses. Only two turns
changed in both replicates, so the unstable cases do not form a fixed
subset that can be removed. We therefore treat the null arm as a noise
floor and accept a change only when its pre-registered target cases
improve while its controls remain stable.

### V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 6: The rule tree and the agent judge on the same 2,169 turns.
Neither bar is the shipped label: the judge overturns only under seven
named rules
(§[V-D](#S5.SS4 "V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")),
so what ships lies between them. The disagreement is concentrated on the
two classes a support desk cares most about: turns blamed on the model,
and turns nobody could attribute.

The rule tree and agent judge disagree on 354 of 2,169 turns (16.3%), as
shown in
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support");
they agree on the other 1,815 turns (83.7%). Where they differ, the
judge assigns fewer turns to model (159 versus 85) and leaves fewer
unattributed (306 versus 205). The largest flows are model
$`\rightarrow`$ no_failure (59), unknown $`\rightarrow`$ knowledge (45),
prompt $`\rightarrow`$ no_failure (36), and model $`\rightarrow`$ prompt
(31). A confidence threshold did not provide an effective override
policy. The reported confidence represents the type and amount of
evidence available, not a calibrated probability that the proposed route
is correct; it was often highest when the judge and tree already agreed.
Policy C in
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
exhibits this limitation, and a later rubric revision was reverted when
evaluation agreement fell from 72% to 66%.

The rule that produced the tree’s route was more informative. On the 98
training turns, the judge alone was correct in ten cases and the tree
alone in seven. The judge was most useful when the tree inferred a route
from missing or weak evidence, because the judge could probe the corpus
for additional evidence. It was less reliable when the tree’s route
followed positive evidence that the judge could not independently
improve.

We therefore use a deterministic, rule-conditioned override gate. In
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support"),
every override policy except the confidence-only gate improves agreement
by 7–9 percentage points on both splits relative to the tree alone. The
evaluation split does not distinguish the three best policies, and the
ungated judge produces fewer spurious knowledge routes than the shipped
policy. Rule conditioning was selected for operational reasons: its
seven conditions are inspectable, its behavior is predictable if judge
quality degrades, and the tree bounds its failure modes. On the complete
expert reference, this gate corrects nine routes without a regression.
These results support using the judge, but do not establish that rule
conditioning is more accurate than accepting every judge proposal.

|     |                                                 |            |           |                    |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------- | --------- | ------------------ |
|     | policy                                          | train (99) | eval (45) | spurious knowledge |
| A   | rule tree alone, no judge                       | 73%        | 64%       | 5                  |
| B   | judge alone, no gate                            | 80%        | 71%       | 1                  |
| C   | judge if confidence $`\geq 0.8`$                | 77%        | 67%       | 2                  |
| D   | judge if the tree fired a weak rule _(shipped)_ | 81%        | 71%       | 5                  |
| E   | D, and confidence $`\geq 0.7`$                  | 82%        | 71%       | 5                  |

TABLE III: Gate policies on the same frozen records, measured earlier in
the campaign, hence $`n{=}99/45`$. “Spurious knowledge” counts turns
wrongly sent to documentation authoring. Bold marks the best value in a
column. D is the policy we ship.

The override gate reuses cached judge proposals and is therefore
deterministic; every pre-registered target must change as expected. Its
authority is limited to routing. Ticket replies, corpus changes, and
pull requests remain subject to expert review regardless of which
component assigns the route.

### V-E RQ4: Do Diagnoses Lead to Effective Repairs?

The final evaluation tests whether a diagnosed failure can guide a
targeted repair. We examine one prompt failure and one knowledge gap.
For each case, the diagnostic identifies the responsible component, a
candidate change is authored, and its effect is measured by replaying
production questions
(Fig. [7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-E RQ4: Do Diagnoses Lead to Effective Repairs? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")).
These are controlled offline experiments; neither change was
automatically promoted to the deployed system.

Each experiment has three arms: _before_ uses the current system,
_after_ changes exactly one component, and _null_ repeats the current
system with the generation cache bypassed. The null arm measures
stochastic variation: in these experiments, an unchanged configuration
altered roughly one quarter of individual responses. Effects are
therefore measured between the after and null arms, which are
independent draws made after target cases have been selected. Comparing
after directly with the selection baseline would overestimate
improvement through regression to the mean.

We require an observed effect to exceed both the change in aggregate
rate and the number of per-turn flips in the null arm. This distinction
matters because opposing changes may cancel in aggregate; in one run,
the rate changed by only $`+0.016`$ although 27 of 188 turns (14.4%)
changed. The primary metrics below are deterministic string matches, so
the repair results do not depend on the agent judge evaluated in RQ3.
Retrieved contexts are frozen for the prompt experiment. For the
knowledge experiment, the candidate document is injected directly,
isolating its potential contribution while intentionally bypassing
retrieval.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 7: One pass of the production loop. Only the first two fix kinds
have been run; a retrieval-side repair is designed and not yet
exercised. An effect is read as _fix against null_, never _fix against
before_: selecting a target set on a stochastic symptom makes the
before-arm rate 1.0 by construction. Numbers are in
§[V-E](#S5.SS5 "V-E RQ4: Do Diagnoses Lead to Effective Repairs? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support").

#### V-E1 Questions and Reference Answers

Both experiments use a frozen question set derived from ALCF traffic.
This choice preserves requests that the existing corpus cannot answer,
whereas questions synthesized from a corpus tend to represent
information already present in that corpus \[[38](#bib.bib13),
[39](#bib.bib27)\]. From 3,495 session snapshots, 2,320 user messages
were deduplicated and consolidated into 1,512 canonical questions. A
bounded-tool agent drafted reference answers using only sources it
opened, after which a human reviewer accepted, edited, or rejected them.
Before experimentation, we content-hashed two subsets: 288 questions for
the prompt repair and 68 for the knowledge repair.

#### V-E2 Repairing a Prompt Failure

Harness analysis identified over-clarification as the largest cluster
assigned to prompt: the assistant asks a follow-up question even when
retrieved evidence is sufficient. We evaluated a change to the
conversation prompt used by 99.5% of traffic.

Across 288 frozen questions and two generation models, the change
significantly reduced clarifying questions relative to the null arm
(Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-E2 Repairing a Prompt Failure ‣ V-E RQ4: Do Diagnoses Lead to Effective Repairs? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")).
Responses became longer and included more citations, indicating that the
reduction was not caused by truncation. The change also increased
under-clarification—cases in which the assistant should have requested
missing system information. Beneficial changes outnumbered adverse
changes by about four to one, but the tradeoff requires expert judgment
before deployment. The control set also changed, so this experiment
cannot distinguish the intended instruction from the effect of modifying
the prompt more generally; a placebo prompt is required to isolate that
mechanism.

#### V-E3 Repairing a Knowledge Gap

The router also identified questions about AI coding assistants for
which a corpus probe found no coverage of five named tools. A
documentation page was drafted and approved by the content owner.
Directly injecting this page raised fact utilization from 0.070 to
0.202, compared with 0.060 when a same-sized unrelated page was
injected. This result isolates the value of the missing content, but
represents an upper bound rather than an end-to-end repair because it
bypasses retrieval and re-indexing.

When the new page was chunked into the offline scoring corpus,
Table [V](#S5.T5 "TABLE V ‣ V-E3 Repairing a Knowledge Gap ‣ V-E RQ4: Do Diagnoses Lead to Effective Repairs? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
showed higher completeness and faithfulness on target questions and
little change on controls for both generation models. Correctness also
rises above its null arm, but we do not claim it: unlike the other two
dimensions it re-retrieves from the scoring corpus, and its null moved
0.072 on one model where theirs moved under 0.01.

The utilization increase supports the knowledge attribution for this
cluster. Across the broader question set, however, 76% of gold facts
missing from retrieved context were already present in the corpus; their
absence was therefore a retrieval failure. The remaining 24% is an upper
bound on genuine documentation gaps, since the offline snapshot is a
subset of the production index. This distinction directs support effort
toward either retrieval improvement or content authoring rather than
treating every missing fact as a request for new documentation.

## VI Discussion and Limitations

Three design lessons are likely to transfer to other facilities. First,
retrieval should be evaluated at both the production-result and corpus
levels; the distinction determines whether a retrieval engineer or
documentation owner can act on the failure. Second, answer-quality
scores should not be treated as repair decisions. A visible symptom does
not uniquely identify the component that caused it, and the reliability
of attribution is bounded by the evidence detectors that feed the
policy. Third, a repair evaluation should measure both the target
behavior and its inverse. The prompt repair reduced unnecessary
clarification but also increased under-clarification, a tradeoff that a
single-direction metric would miss.

The study has several limitations. All labelled data come from the ALCF,
and approximately two thirds of the 150-turn reference received only one
expert label. The class distribution is unbalanced, making per-route
estimates unreliable for rare model, unknown, and tools_mcp cases. We
report exact agreement without a chance-corrected statistic, and the
held-out split contains only 52 turns. The gate-policy comparison in
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-D RQ3: What Does the Agent Judge Contribute? ‣ V Evaluation ‣ AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System forIntelligent HPC User Support")
is the only agentic-versus-deterministic control. Finally, each repair
study represents one experimental campaign. Null arms estimate
run-to-run variation but do not substitute for repeated independent
trials.

The implemented system also stops short of fully autonomous repair.
Three of the five failure routes have not been exercised through an
end-to-end repair path, and no generated knowledge change has been
merged and re-indexed in the deployed corpus. The remaining errors,
rejected harness arms, and finding that 76% of missing retrieved facts
already exist in the corpus all identify retrieval quality as the
highest-priority next step.

## VII Conclusion

Deploying a RAG assistant creates a corresponding operational challenge:
determining why an answer failed and who can repair it. AskALCF
addresses this challenge by evaluating answer quality separately from
retrieval sufficiency and by testing retrieval at both the
production-result and corpus levels. This distinction separates missing
documentation from failed retrieval and converts quality evidence into a
component-level work item.

Across 2,174 production turns, the router assigned a failure mode to
1,295 turns and explicitly left 309 unattributed. Human-guided harness
training increased agreement with a 150-turn expert reference from 108
to 123 turns, including an increase from 67% to 77% on a
session-disjoint evaluation split. An agent judge provided useful
independent evidence when the rule tree reasoned from missing
information; a rule-conditioned gate bounded its authority more
effectively than a confidence threshold.

The expert-review interface is central to this improvement process. It
produces the reference labels used for evaluation and captures
rationales that motivate bounded changes to rules, prompts, and
knowledge. Controlled repair studies showed that diagnoses can guide
prompt and documentation changes, while also revealing adverse effects
that require expert judgment.

The system therefore demonstrates a governed path from support
interactions to measured improvement, but not a fully closed autonomous
loop. Candidate repairs have been evaluated offline; generated knowledge
changes have not yet been merged and re-indexed in production.
Completing and evaluating that final stage is future work.
